sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Yavapai County
sections.html:
Property tax here is split between two county offices. Value comes from the Assessor, who appraises every parcel. Billing and collecting belong to the Treasurer, who then passes the money to the county, Yavapai College, school and fire districts, special districts and cities. The Board of Supervisors sets tax rates after the taxing districts submit their budgets and levies each August.

The Treasurer's Office has a counter in Prescott at 1015 Fair Street, 2nd floor, phone (928) 771-3233, with weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday. The Cottonwood Annex, 10 S 6th Street, phone (928) 639-8123, keeps shorter hours: Monday through Thursday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., with a closure from noon to 1:00 p.m. and none at all on Friday. Email goes to web.treasurer@yavapaiaz.gov. For valuation and exemption questions, call the Assessor at (928) 771-3220.

Your bill carries a four-digit tax area code. Every parcel in the same code pays the same mix of jurisdictions, which always includes the county, the community college and one or more school districts, and may add a city, fire district or improvement district. Two houses a few miles apart can therefore carry different rates, and a house in Chino Valley, Camp Verde or Sedona can sit in a different tax area from one in Prescott Valley. Find the code printed on your own bill.

The year's tax is split into two payments. A.R.S. 42-18052 puts one due October 1 and the other the next March 1, and a payment is late once 5:00 p.m. passes on November 1 or May 1 respectively. If that date is a weekend or holiday, lateness begins at 5:00 p.m. the next business day.

DateWhat happens
By March 1Assessor mails Notices of Value
End of SeptemberPaper tax notices mailed
December 31, 2026Last day to pay the full year with no charged interest
February 9, 2027Next online tax lien auction
May 3, 2027, 5:00 p.m.Second half delinquent (May 1 falls on a Saturday)

The Treasurer cannot change or extend statutory due dates, and the payment system will not take money before bills are calculated in late September.

Once tax is delinquent it earns simple interest of 16 percent a year, and any part of a month is charged as a full month (A.R.S. 42-18053). Two cases avoid interest: paying the whole year by December 31 of the tax year, and a delinquency caused by an assessor or treasurer mistake. With Board of Supervisors approval, the treasurer can also waive interest one time per property when the delinquency falls within a year after a mortgage or deed of trust is released.

sections.h2: How to pay a Yavapai County tax bill
sections.html:
Four ways to pay exist: online, phone, mail and counter. The online and phone channels run through Certified Payments, and the fees go to that vendor, not to the Treasurer. Phone payments use 1-866-493-0416.

  • Electronic check: $0.40 per transaction, and one e-check can cover several parcels
  • Debit card: 1 percent of the amount, minimum $1.25
  • Credit card: 2.19 percent of the amount, minimum $1.25
  • Mail: Yavapai County Treasurer, 1015 Fair St., Prescott, AZ 86305, with the parcel number on the check
  • In person: the Prescott or Cottonwood counter

Mail takes three to five business days to post, and electronic payments take three. Pay the exact amount, because an overpayment is refunded. Owners who want paper bills replaced can register at eNoticesOnline with the authorization code on the front of the last bill.

What you owe also works as a lien on the property. Per A.R.S. 42-17153 it arises on January 1 of the tax year and ranks above other liens and encumbrances, except state liens and liens for other years' taxes.

Yavapai County runs an annual online tax lien auction, and the next is set for February 9, 2027. Properties deeded to the state for back taxes are offered separately on the Board of Supervisors' Tax Deed Sales page. A seller with delinquent years should remember that interest runs at 16 percent and the lien sale happens each February.

Your Notice of Value, mailed by March 1, prints a filing date for a Petition for Review to the Assessor, and the window runs 60 days from the postmark. Petition forms are available from the Assessor's website during the filing period or at either Assessor office, and they come with instructions.

  • Notice of Change: mailed by September 30 for new construction, additions, splits or changes in use. Take it to the County Board of Equalization within 25 days of mailing. A state-certified hearing officer hears the appeal.
  • Tax Court: if you disagree with the Assessor or the Board, file within 60 days of the Board's decision or by December 15, whichever is later.
  • Skip the administrative step: you may file directly in Tax Court, but no later than December 15 of the valuation year.
  • Buyers: if you bought before December 15 of the valuation year, you may appeal to Tax Court by that date. Later, the new owner has until December 15 of the levy year.

Full Cash Value is the appealable figure. Your tax is actually computed from the Limited Property Value. That figure can climb only 5 percent a year unless the property changed, and 95 percent of Yavapai parcels fall in that group.

Personal exemption applications are taken in person at either Assessor office on weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The season runs from the first Monday in January through the last business day of February. Exemptions cover widows and widowers, totally and permanently disabled persons, disabled military service members and their surviving spouses.

The rules for a disabled service member are changing. Someone with a 100 percent service-connected disability, or total disability based on individual unemployability, gets a full exemption on the primary residence starting with tax year 2026, with income limits still applying that year. Legislation passed in 2026 removes the income limit beginning with tax year 2027. Others who qualify receive the annual exemption amount the state sets. The Senior Freeze program closes to applicants on September 1.

Owner-occupied homes already receive a State Aid reduction on the primary school district tax, shown on the bill, and the state reimburses the school districts. Ask the Assessor at (928) 771-3220 which documents to bring, including an Arizona driver's license and a VA award letter for a disability claim.

Before listing, find out from the Treasurer what the parcel owes, and plan to clear it through escrow at closing. The county's tax inquiry website lets you search by parcel number and view a bill. Whoever owns the house while taxes are due is responsible for them. A bill that lands after the sale goes to the new owner or the mortgage company.

Pricing is part of the conversation. The 2026 median single-family price is $539,000 through October, down from $555,000 in 2025, so check the tax area on your bill and compare your house with recent sales near it.

A typical closing runs in order: the title company requests a payoff from the Treasurer, you and the buyer sign, escrow pays the open amount from your proceeds, and the deed is recorded. Bring your latest tax notice and parcel number.

faqs.q: When is the second half of Yavapai County property tax due?
faqs.a: March 1 is the due date. Under A.R.S. 42-18052 it is late after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, and since May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, lateness starts at 5:00 p.m. Monday, May 3, 2027. Paying the full year by December 31 means no charged interest.

faqs.q: How much interest does Yavapai County charge on late property tax?
faqs.a: Sixteen percent simple interest per year, counting any part of a month as a full one (A.R.S. 42-18053). Interest is not charged when the full year is paid by December 31 of the tax year, or when an assessor or treasurer error caused the delinquency.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Yavapai County property value?
faqs.a: Count 60 days from the postmark on the Notice of Value mailed by March 1. A Notice of Change, mailed by September 30, gives you 25 days from mailing to reach the County Board of Equalization. December 15 is the usual Tax Court cutoff.

faqs.q: Who pays property tax when a Yavapai County house sells?
faqs.a: Taxes due fall on the current owner, and escrow usually pays the open amount at closing. A bill that arrives after the sale is paid by the new owner or mortgage company. Get the parcel's balance from the Treasurer first.

faqs.q: Can I pay Yavapai County property tax by credit card?
faqs.a: Yes. Certified Payments charges 2.19 percent with a $1.25 minimum for credit cards, 1 percent with a $1.25 minimum for debit cards, and $0.40 for an electronic check. The fee goes to the vendor, not the Treasurer. Pay online from the Treasurer's page or call 1-866-493-0416.
